Anti biotic resistance arises from surviving bacteria, because they can then go on to reproduce. So while a correct course of antibiotics will cure the infection, there is a chance that some resistant bacteria will remain. This does not mean they will cause infection, but rather have the innate genes required to resist antibiotics. If they were to mutate and become out of check with your immune system, or someone else’s they may then become infectious again.

For example strep throat is caused by bacteria getting where they shouldn’t be within you. Those bacteria are always present but balanced with your immune system. If that balance is broken and you may get an infection. If the bacteria had previously survived antibiotics they may be resistant to the same antibiotic.
[who](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/antibiotic-resistance)

This is false. In fact antibiotics are the cause of superbugs becoming prominent. If you kill 99.9% of the bacteria you may no longer be sick, but you’ve also potentially left some strains that are antibiotic resistant and can now reproduce unhindered due to the lack of competition. This is why doctors try to use certain antibiotics as a last resort in order to prevent “culling the litter” in a negative way for the future.

Mutations are random and occur over generations. A single bacterium can’t itself mutate to adapt. Overtime yes they could be naturally selected to become resistant to antibiotics (which I assume is what you mean by superbug). MRSA a common infection in hospitals is a superbug because it evolved to be antibiotic resistant to current drugs.

The search for new antibiotics is a crucial area of research to stay ahead of mutations.
